candidates.title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
candidates.raw_content: Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :) What it does today: - Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router. - Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks. - Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance. We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results. But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now. We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions: - 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency) -The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps. Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels. So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8. The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections. You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results: https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega... Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback. Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai. We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50533270 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

candidates.title: Show HN: AI Spar – Turn conflicting AI answers into a structured debate
candidates.raw_content: Over the last couple of years, I have observed many people (including myself) researching tricky topics by asking the same question to multiple AI's. If those answers conflict, we manually copy the answers back-and-forth between the AI apps to make them debate each other, to get a fuller picture of the topic. I developed AI Spar to organize and automate this debate process. When the user asks a question: 1) Multiple AI's answer the question independent of each other. 2) An analyzer (also an AI model) finds the consensuses and disagreements between those answers, and what important points are missed by which answer. 3) For each disagreement point, each AI tries to defend its stance when presented with its original answer and the other side's opinion (it can concede if it feels the other side is right); and for each missed point, each AI tries to clarify whether it agrees with the point. 4) If all disagreement points have consensus, or the debate has reached max number of rounds, then go to 5); otherwise, go to 3) for the next round of debate with the latest arguments from each side. 5) The analyzer summarizes the debate, synthesizes a final answer, and lists the consensus points, resolved disagreements, unresolved disagreements, and clarified missed points. Note that it might feel slow compared to those AI apps, because of all the steps taken above. Also worth a disclaimer: even if all AI's eventually agree on one point, that doesn't necessarily mean it's correct. Some friends have been testing this system. They mention that sometimes reading the back-and-forth debate details is a lot more fun than reading the final synthesis. Without signing in, you can try two separate questions, with entry-level models from 3 AI providers (Gemini, GPT, Claude). Signing in enables additional features: asking follow-up questions, attaching images or PDFs, saving and sharing conversations. Also, stronger models from these providers are available for signed-in users. In addition, you can enable web-search grounded debates, and optional fact-checking during the debates. You pay as you go, no subscription at this point. Cost of each debate depends on the models and settings. We also support BYOK for these providers, with a separate system fee. CLI/API access is also available if you need them. An interesting debate example: https://aispar.app/share/5f503127-4b4a-4c5c-9b2a-74081016b68... "Should junior developers use coding agents from their first day? " Even though all three AI's (Gemini, GPT, Claude) initially broadly agree on the surface, after the debate, each has made pretty big changes on the substance, and at the end there's still unresolved disagreement. candidates.title: The chart of token spend per employee still has no ceiling in sight. And the closer you are to AI right now the deeper the sense is that we’re actually still in the early part of the curve of token use and adoption. This summer and fall’s model releases have continued to push the state of the art forward at a rate that already felt hard to maintain. As a result, for most productive use-cases the models are only now starting to actually work, and the feeling is that things will only accelerate from here. Coding, in retrospect, was basically trash even 12 months ago. Now it’s finally starting to get good. And now that coding is actually working, you’re getting tool and computer use, which open up a wide variety of knowledge work domains that weren’t possible to throw agents at before. Once you have agents that can code, use computers, leverage any tool out there, and understand a variety of domains, you can begin to throw them at a wide variety of knowledge work tasks that were hard to bring automation to across finance, life sciences, cyber, and more. So that brings agents to a broad set of work that we’re not really using them in yet at scale. Then comes the new form factors of agents. Agent swarms and background agents are going to eat up vastly more tokens than anything we can imagine. You’ll have agents running in most enterprises workflows processing data, validating work, doing research, providing decision support, and so on. And we’ll have swarms that fan out in parallel in areas like cyber, life sciences, coding, and more. So basically tokens are only going up from here.

candidates.title: My top 5 takeaways from @nateparrott on how to get Claude to design without AI slop: 1. Give Claude context upfront. Share screenshots, pages you like, and your past work. For an existing product, have Claude rebuild the real screens from code. 2. Research familiar UX patterns. For hard layout problems, ask Claude to research familiar products that solve something similar and note the layouts people already know how to use. 3. Make Claude aware of its design biases. "The model has no idea what its own biases are." In your design.md or another file, consider discouraging Claude's tells like serif text, off-white backgrounds, and card-edge bars. 4. Start with wireframes. Have Claude create wireframes first and give it feedback to nail your core user flows before going deep on fonts and colors. 5. Ask for multiple options, then remix them. Ask Claude for 5 options for key screens with different fonts, colors, and styles. Then pick the parts you like and ask it to remix and create 5 more options. 📌 Watch the full episode now: https://t.co/HPX5HjXafX Also available as a written post: https://t.co/jcofmkQc01
